steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the disparate impact of pruning: sparse models lose accuracy unevenly across sub-groups, and we propose a constrained optimization approach to control it. Cover the problem, why existing mitigation methods fall short, our formulation, the contributions, and the generalization caveat.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction
- Large models and the need for compression
- Disparate impact of pruning on sub-groups
- Limitations of existing mitigation methods
- Our approach: constraints on excess accuracy gaps (CEAG), Fig. 1
- Contributions
- Caveat: failure to generalize to unseen data

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction
- Large models, compression
  - trend toward larger architectures (cite); GPT-4, Llama 2, DALL-E 2 (cite each)
  - compression: pruning, knowledge distillation, quantization (cite each)
  - needed to deploy large models on many platforms, incl. resource-constrained edge devices like smartphones
- Disparate impact
  - pruned models comparable on aggregate over whole dataset, but big accuracy drop for some sub-groups (cite x3)
  - under-represented groups degrade a lot while overall performance unaffected -> worsens systemic biases
  - prior work calls this "disparate impact of pruning" (cite)
- Existing mitigation
  - problems: interpretability, scaling to many sub-groups
  - equalized loss constraints across sub-groups for sparse model (cite) -> ignores unequal group-level performance of the dense model; loss = useful surrogate but indirect, controls loss not group-level accuracy changes
  - per-group importance scores for every parameter to pick weights to prune (cite) -> prohibitively expensive with large model or many sub-groups
- Our approach
  - characterize disparate impact as group-level accuracy gaps between dense and sparse models
  - formulation: constraints on per-group excess accuracy gaps (CEAG)
  - interpretable semantics: feasible solutions = low pruning-induced disparity
  - negligible overhead vs. naive (disparity-agnostic) fine-tuning of sparse model (Section E.1) -> works with many groups, e.g. intersectional fairness
  - Fig. 1: disparity as excess accuracy gaps (EAGs, § 3.1); naive fine-tuning hurts group Others disproportionately; equalized loss mitigates; ours consistently reduces disparity; § 5
- Contributions
  - CEAG constrained problem (§ 3), bounds group-level accuracy gaps dense vs. sparse
  - algorithm for non-differentiable, stochastic constraints (§ 4): proxy constraints (cite) for non-differentiability; replay buffers (§ 4.2) for noisy constraint estimates
  - replay buffers also improve training dynamics of equalized loss formulation (cite) -> better models in terms of disparity
  - experiments: multiple architectures, datasets, sparsity levels (§ 5); intersectional groups, up to hundreds of constraints
- Caveat
  - all methods incl. ours fail to mitigate disparities on unseen data
  - first to document this generalization challenge (as far as we know)
  - still a step in the right direction: only method that reliably mitigates on training set
  - hope to motivate research on generalization of mitigation methods

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Current deep learning practice shows a trend toward larger architectures, for example popular models like GPT-4, Llama 2 and DALL-E 2. Model compression techniques like pruning, knowledge distillation, or quantization are crucial for deploying large models across a wide range of platforms, including resource-constrained edge devices like smartphones.

Even though they get comparable performance at an aggregate level over the whole dataset, pruned models often show a significant reduction in accuracy for some data sub-groups. In particular, under-represented groups can suffer a high degradation in performance while the overall performance is not affected, and this makes systemic biases in machine learning models worse. Prior work calls this phenomenon the disparate impact of pruning.

The existing mitigation methods have problems with interpretability and with scaling to a large number of sub-groups. One previous method introduces constraints that try to equalize the loss of the sparse model across sub-groups. But this approach doesn't take into account that the dense model also has unequal performance at the group level. Also, the loss can be a useful surrogate for training, but this method only deals with the disparate impact issue indirectly, because it focuses on controlling the loss and not the changes in accuracy at the group level. Alternatively, another method computes per-group importance scores for every model parameter to decide which weights get pruned. This approach gets prohibitively expensive when the model or the number of sub-groups is large.

In this work we characterize the disparate impact of pruning in terms of the accuracy gaps at the group level between the dense and sparse models. We also propose a problem formulation that addresses the disparate impact of pruning directly by putting constraints on the per-group excess accuracy gaps (CEAG). A key advantage of our formulation is that it has interpretable semantics: the feasible solutions of our optimization problem correspond to models with low pruning-induced disparity. Finally, our approach adds a negligible computational overhead (Section E.1) compared to naive (disparity-agnostic) fine-tuning of the sparse model, so it can be applied to problems with large numbers of groups, like intersectional fairness tasks.

- Fig. 1: disparity as excess accuracy gaps (EAGs, § 3.1); naive fine-tuning hurts group Others disproportionately; equalized loss mitigates; ours consistently reduces disparity; see § 5
- Contributions
  - CEAG constrained problem (§ 3), bounds group-level accuracy gaps dense vs. sparse
  - algorithm for non-differentiable, stochastic constraints (§ 4): proxy constraints for non-differentiability; replay buffers (§ 4.2) for noisy constraint estimates
  - replay buffers improve training dynamics of the equalized loss formulation -> better models in terms of disparity
  - experiments: multiple architectures, datasets, sparsity levels (§ 5); intersectional groups, up to hundreds of constraints
- Caveat: all methods incl. ours fail on unseen data; first to document it; ours only one reliable on training set; hope it motivates research on generalization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Current deep learning practice shows a trend toward larger architectures, for example popular models like GPT-4, Llama 2 and DALL-E 2. Model compression techniques like pruning, knowledge distillation, or quantization are crucial for deploying large models across a wide range of platforms, including resource-constrained edge devices like smartphones.

Even though they get comparable performance at an aggregate level over the whole dataset, pruned models often show a significant reduction in accuracy for some data sub-groups. In particular, under-represented groups can suffer a high degradation in performance while the overall performance is not affected, and this makes systemic biases in machine learning models worse. Prior work calls this phenomenon the disparate impact of pruning.

The existing mitigation methods have problems with interpretability and with scaling to a large number of sub-groups. One previous method introduces constraints that try to equalize the loss of the sparse model across sub-groups. But this approach doesn't take into account that the dense model also has unequal performance at the group level. Also, the loss can be a useful surrogate for training, but this method only deals with the disparate impact issue indirectly, because it focuses on controlling the loss and not the changes in accuracy at the group level. Alternatively, another method computes per-group importance scores for every model parameter to decide which weights get pruned. This approach gets prohibitively expensive when the model or the number of sub-groups is large.

In this work we characterize the disparate impact of pruning in terms of the accuracy gaps at the group level between the dense and sparse models. We also propose a problem formulation that addresses the disparate impact of pruning directly by putting constraints on the per-group excess accuracy gaps (CEAG). A key advantage of our formulation is that it has interpretable semantics: the feasible solutions of our optimization problem correspond to models with low pruning-induced disparity. Finally, our approach adds a negligible computational overhead (Section E.1) compared to naive (disparity-agnostic) fine-tuning of the sparse model, so it can be applied to problems with large numbers of groups, like intersectional fairness tasks.

Fig. 1 shows how reliable our approach is at mitigating the disparate impact of pruning. We measure disparity with excess accuracy gaps (EAGs, § 3.1). Naive fine-tuning gives models that affect group Others disproportionately, and the equalized loss formulation mitigates the issue, but our formulation consistently reduces the pruning-induced disparity. See § 5 for more discussion.

The main contributions of our work are the following:

- • We formulate a constrained optimization problem (CEAG, § 3) which directly controls disparate impact by bounding the accuracy gaps at the group level between the dense and sparse models.

- • We propose an algorithm to solve constrained optimization problems with non-differentiable, stochastic constraints (§ 4). We use proxy constraints to deal with non-differentiablity, and we introduce replay buffers (§ 4.2) to handle noise in the estimation of the constraints.

- • Our replay buffers make the training dynamics of the equalized loss formulation proposed in prior work better. The better dynamics lead to better models in terms of disparity.

- • Our experiments show that we can reliably mitigate the disparate impact of pruning across multiple architectures, datasets, and sparsity levels (§ 5). These results also hold for tasks with intersectional groups, and up to hundreds of constraints.

Our experimental results show that all the methods considered in this paper (ours included) fail to mitigate pruning-induced disparities on unseen data. As far as we know, we are the first to document this generalization challenge. Still, our proposed method is a step in the right direction, since our approach is the only one that reliably mitigates the disparate impact of pruning on the training set. We hope our empirical observations will motivate more research on improving the generalization properties of methods for mitigating the disparate impact of pruning.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Current deep learning practice displays a trend towards larger architectures [1], as exemplified by popular models such as GPT-4 [2], Llama 2 [3] and DALL-E 2 [4]. Model compression techniques such as pruning [5], knowledge distillation [6], or quantization [7] are crucial for enabling the deployment of large models across a wide range of platforms, including resource-constrained edge devices like smartphones.

Despite achieving comparable performance at an aggregate level over the entire dataset, pruned models often show significant accuracy reduction for some data sub-groups [8,9,10]. In particular, under-represented groups can suffer high performance degradation while the overall performance remains unaffected, which exacerbates systemic biases in machine learning models. [11] refer to this phenomenon as the disparate impact of pruning.

Existing mitigation methods face challenges in terms of interpretability and scalability to a large number of sub-groups. [11] introduce constraints that aim to equalize the loss of the sparse model across sub-groups. However, their approach does not account for the unequal group-level performance of the dense model. Moreover, while the loss can be a useful surrogate for training, this method addresses the disparate impact issue only indirectly, as it focuses on controlling the loss rather than group-level changes in accuracy. Alternatively, [12] compute per-group importance scores for every model parameter to determine which weights to prune. This approach becomes prohibitively expensive when the model or the number of sub-groups is large.

In this work, we characterize the disparate impact of pruning in terms of the group-level accuracy gaps between the dense and sparse models. We also propose a problem formulation that directly addresses the disparate impact of pruning by imposing constraints on the per-group excess accuracy gaps (CEAG). A key advantage of our formulation is its interpretable semantics: feasible solutions of our optimization problem correspond to models with low pruning-induced disparity. Finally, our approach introduces a negligible computational overhead (Section E.1) compared to (disparity-agnostic) naive fine-tuning of the sparse model, which makes it applicable to problems with large numbers of groups, such as intersectional fairness tasks.

Fig. 1 illustrates the reliability of our approach at mitigating the disparate impact of pruning. We measure disparity in terms of excess accuracy gaps (EAGs, § 3.1). Naive fine-tuning yields models that disproportionately affect group Others; the equalized loss formulation mitigates the issue, but our formulation consistently reduces the pruning-induced disparity. See § 5 for further discussion.

The main contributions of our work are as follows:

- • We formulate a constrained optimization problem (CEAG, § 3) that directly controls disparate impact by bounding group-level accuracy gaps between the dense and sparse models.

- • We propose an algorithm for solving constrained optimization problems with non-differentiable, stochastic constraints (§ 4). We use proxy constraints [13] to address non-differentiablity, and introduce replay buffers (§ 4.2) to handle noise in the estimation of constraints.

- • Our replay buffers improve the training dynamics of the equalized loss formulation proposed by [11], which leads to better models in terms of disparity.

- • Our experiments demonstrate that we can reliably mitigate the disparate impact of pruning across multiple architectures, datasets, and sparsity levels (§ 5). These results carry over to tasks with intersectional groups, and to up to hundreds of constraints.

Our experimental results indicate that all methods considered in this paper (including ours) fail to mitigate pruning-induced disparities on unseen data. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to document this generalization challenge. Nevertheless, our proposed method is a step in the right direction, since it is the only approach that reliably mitigates the disparate impact of pruning on the training set. We hope our empirical observations will motivate further research on improving the generalization properties of methods for mitigating the disparate impact of pruning.
